title: Yen Steadies After Breaching 160; US Dollar Index Hits 19-Month High, Euro Falls to 1.5-Year Low — BigGo Finance
html:
In early trading in the Tokyo foreign exchange market on Monday, the US Dollar Index briefly climbed to 103.441, setting a new high since April 8, 2025 — a more than 19-month record. The euro weakened in tandem, dipping intraday to $1.1017, an roughly 19-month low since April 10, 2025, before paring losses slightly to around $1.1025. The yen hovered near the flat line, trading at ¥159.69 to the dollar and ¥176.04 to the euro, with limited movement.

The driver behind this bout of dollar strength was a hawkish shift in US monetary policy. Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmid said on Sunday that the Federal Reserve "still has work to do on inflation." He is not a voting member of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) this year, but his remarks nonetheless reinforced market expectations for a faster pace of tightening.

Interest rate futures pricing adjusted accordingly. The CME FedWatch tool showed the market sees a 93.9% probability that the Federal Reserve will raise rates by a quarter point at its two-day meeting ending December 9, while the probability of a half-point hike fell to 6% from 11.5% last Friday. Traders are also betting on a cumulative four rate hikes by September next year, though the magnitude differences are small. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury note edged down 0.8 basis points to 5.143%.

In Japan, the Cabinet Office reported Monday that real gross domestic product (GDP) for July to September 2026 contracted 0.1% on an annualized basis in the preliminary reading, not only below market expectations of 0.2% to 0.3% growth but also the first negative growth in four quarters. Household consumption was the biggest drag, falling 0.3% for the quarter; net exports subtracted 0.6 percentage points from growth as import costs rose. Corporate investment bucked the trend with 1.6% growth, as artificial intelligence (AI)-related demand continued to support capital spending. The Bank of Japan's October Tankan survey also showed that large companies plan to increase fixed asset investment by 11.3% in the fiscal year ending March 2027.

In its latest "Outlook for Economic Activity and Prices" report, the Bank of Japan attributed part of the consumption weakness to weather, citing typhoons, heavy rain and consecutive days of rainfall that suppressed household spending; rising living costs also made consumers more cautious. Higher import energy prices and import prices pushed up by a weak yen also eroded domestic demand momentum.

Paradoxically, the poor economic data did not drag the yen to a further low. The yen had weakened to ¥160.19 to the dollar last Friday, the lowest since September 2, but did not extend its decline on Monday. Market vigilance over intervention by the Japanese government and the Bank of Japan to buy yen became an invisible support for the currency. However, expectations that the US-Japan interest rate differential will be slow to narrow also brought dollar buying to the surface from time to time, and the yen briefly turned weaker intraday.

Capital Economics said in a report that the third-quarter economic stagnation "probably will not prevent the Bank of Japan from tightening policy further at its December meeting," and believes that with inflation about to surge, the pace of central bank tightening may exceed its previous estimates.

Major investment banks' views on the yen's outlook diverge markedly. Morgan Stanley strategist Serena Tang's team forecasts the yen will weaken to 162 to the dollar by the fourth quarter of 2027, citing strong global risk appetite, deteriorating Japanese terms of trade and the appeal of carry trades, which will outweigh the support to the yen from a narrowing US-Japan rate differential. The bank also believes the market may continue to perceive the Bank of Japan's policy pace as lagging behind economic conditions, which would limit the boost to the yen from rising domestic Japanese interest rates.

Goldman Sachs strategist Kamakshya Trivedi's team takes the opposite side. The bank forecasts the dollar-yen pair at 158 in three months, 155 in six months and 150 in a year, and says its preferred fair value gauge shows the yen is currently undervalued by about 30%. Goldman economists believe the Bank of Japan has adjusted its rate hike pace to once per quarter and expect three more hikes of 25 basis points each, bringing the policy rate to 2% by June 2027, above the roughly 1.75% currently priced by the market.

Another basis for Goldman's bullish yen view is the potential repatriation of Japanese capital, among which any adjustment to the asset allocation of the Government Pension Investment Fund (GPIF) would be a bellwether for other investors. However, the bank also acknowledged that such a shift is currently "more of a possibility than a reality that has already occurred"; investors tracking overseas asset exposure without currency hedging have overall continued to increase demand for overseas assets this year, with no clear signs of repatriation to the Japanese domestic market as of October.

Among other major currencies, the pound traded at $1.3216, down 0.01% and falling for a fifth consecutive trading day, with $1.3137 on October 14 marking a recent low; the Australian dollar traded at $0.6777 and the New Zealand dollar at $0.5523, both little changed. In cryptocurrency markets, Bitcoin rose 0.2% to $65,186.44, stabilizing after three days of selling pressure that took it to a four-month low over the weekend; Ether rose 0.7% to $1,830.94.

Overall, the core variable in this round of currency market moves remains the US interest rate path. Hot inflation data combined with hawkish talk from Federal Reserve officials pushed the US Dollar Index to a 19-month high, pressuring non-US currencies broadly. Although the yen is protected by intervention expectations, the battle around the 160 level remains in focus until the US-Japan rate differential actually narrows; the euro, meanwhile, can hardly shake off the shadow of its 1.5-year low in the near term under a dollar-only strength regime. For investors, the magnitude of the Bank of Japan's tightening at its December meeting and the capital flows of large institutions such as the GPIF will be the two key indicators for judging whether the yen can reverse its decline.
